extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties in PTAB inter partes review proceedings (petitioners and patent owners), and judges/clerks handling motions to amend
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria the Patent Trial and Appeal Board applies when evaluating a patent owner's motion to amend claims in an inter partes review (35 U.S.C. §316(d); 37 C.F.R. §42.121), and related patentability and evidentiary rules (indefiniteness, enablement, obviousness, objective indicia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable number of substitute claims
rubrics_metrics.description: In reviewing a motion to amend, the patent owner must demonstrate the amendment proposes a reasonable number of substitute claims (35 U.S.C. §316(d); 37 C.F.R. §42.121).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of the statutory/regulatory gatekeeping requirements (cited together with the other three requirements). The Board cites Lectrosonics (precedential) for guidance on motions to amend. No specific numeric ceiling is given on the page; reasonableness is evaluated in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment responds to a ground of unpatentability involved in the trial
rubrics_metrics.description: The amendment must respond to a ground of unpatentability involved in the trial (35 U.S.C. §316(d); 37 C.F.R. §42.121).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposed substitute claim must be tailored to address the adjudicated grounds. The Board evaluates whether the new claim scope bears on the grounds asserted in the IPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment does not enlarge claim scope or introduce new subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The amendment must not seek to enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new subject matter (35 U.S.C. §316(d); 37 C.F.R. §42.121).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board reviews both whether the amendment broadens the claims and whether it adds matter beyond the originally filed disclosure; this is a statutory/regulatory requirement cited in Lectrosonics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed claims supported in the original disclosure (no new matter / written description)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed substitute claims must be supported in the original disclosure of the patent (35 U.S.C. §316(d); 37 C.F.R. §42.121).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the written-description/new-matter requirement. The Board examines whether the specification as filed provides adequate support for the claim language; lack of support can justify denial of a motion to amend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of persuasion regarding patentability of substitute claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner does not bear the burden of persuasion to demonstrate the patentability of proposed substitute claims; ordinarily the burden of persuasion will lie with the petitioner to show that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable by a preponderance of the evidence (citing Lectrosonics; Aqua Prods.; Bosch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the patent owner must satisfy the §316(d)/§42.121 requirements, the petitioner ordinarily must demonstrate unpatentability of substitute claims. The Board applies the ordinary preponderance standard to petitioner's challenges to substitute claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests to cancel claims are not contingent
rubrics_metrics.description: A request to cancel claims will not be regarded as contingent (Lectrosonics, precedential).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent owner requests cancellation of original claims as part of a motion to amend, the Board treats that cancellation request as effective/unconditional, not contingent on grant of substitute claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness standard (Nautilus reasonable certainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are indefinite if they fail to 'inform, with reasonable certainty, those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention' (Nautilus, Inc. v. Biosig Instruments, Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board applies Nautilus and related USPTO guidance (USPTO Memorandum on Indefiniteness Under 35 U.S.C. §112 in AIA Post-Grant Proceedings, MPEP 2173.05(e)). Example on this page: a comparative term like 'typical grocery store sugar' can render claims indefinite if it admits multiple reasonable meanings and no 'informed and confident choice' is available among them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative claim terms must be well-defined for comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim compares a property of the claimed invention to a comparator (e.g., 'more completely and consistently dissolved in comparison to the use of typical grocery store sugar'), the comparator must be sufficiently definite so a person of ordinary skill can make the required comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will find such comparative claim language indefinite if the comparator term is ambiguous in scope (multiple plausible definitions, brand-to-brand variance, no numerical standard) such that no 'informed and confident choice' exists. The decision analyzes particle-size distributions and shows that brand variance of EFG sugar made the comparator ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement under 35 U.S.C. §112(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed substitute claims must be enabled by the patent disclosure; petitioners may challenge lack of enablement as a ground for unpatentability (35 U.S.C. §112(a) / enablement issues raised in the proceeding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board considers evidence and expert testimony regarding whether the specification enables the full scope of the proposed claims. The decision discusses enablement in connection with challenges and reference teachings (e.g., arguments that Thijssen is non-enabling for the claimed context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness analysis: teach/suggest, motivation to combine, and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: To show obviousness, the petitioner must demonstrate (1) the cited references teach or suggest the claim limitations, (2) a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine the references, and (3) a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success in doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board applies the Graham framework (and weighs evidence accordingly). The decision applies this standard to combinations (e.g., Cooper combined with Thijssen and conventional practices) and explains why the Board found the necessary teaching/suggestion, motivation, and reasonable expectation of success for certain proposed claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art / pertinence requirement for references
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art reference is only appropriate to consider in an obviousness combination if it is from the same field of endeavor or is reasonably pertinent to the problem the inventor was trying to solve (i.e., analogous art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board evaluates whether references like Thijssen are analogous art by asking if they are in the same field or reasonably pertinent; arguments that a reference addresses industrial coffee packed-bed extraction (not restaurant iced-tea brewing) go to non-analogous-art objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board identifies and adopts a level of ordinary skill in the art for the proceeding, which frames how a person of ordinary skill would understand disclosures, claim terms, and combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision maintains the level of skill set in the Institution Decision (experience/education in the food industry sufficient to understand sugar particle size and screening). Parties may dispute the identified level; the Board may ask parties to brief the issue. The PHOSITA definition informs indefiniteness, enablement, and obviousness analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia (secondary considerations) and nexus requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicia to be considered include long-felt but unmet need, commercial success, copying, praise, skepticism, and unexpected results. To use such evidence, the patentee must show a nexus between the evidence and the claimed features (nexus presumption applies in limited circumstances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board evaluates objective indicia critically: commercial success requires a defined market and a showing that sales represent a substantial portion of that market; sales figures alone are insufficient without market context. A nexus presumption may apply when the evidence is tied to a specific product that is coextensive with the claims (Fox Factory), but without such linkage the patentee must demonstrate direct ties. Copying requires proof of access and similarity (internal documents, photos, disassembly) and praise should specifically relate to claimed features; mere assertions or incorporation-by-reference citations are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation and effect of unchallenged institution findings
rubrics_metrics.description: If petitioners present convincing evidence of anticipation at institution and the patent owner fails to respond or rebut in later briefing, the Board may maintain its institution findings that a reference anticipates original claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision adopts prior Institution Decision findings regarding Cooper's anticipation of original claims where Patent Owner did not submit a Preliminary Response; absence of contrary evidence or arguments can lead the Board to adopt earlier determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural/evidentiary rule for submissions and incorporation by reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must support assertions with specific discussion of exhibits; merely directing the Board to review exhibits without incorporation or argument can violate rules and be unpersuasive (37 C.F.R. §42.6(a) / incorporation by reference constraints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board criticized Patent Owner for directing the Board to review exhibits on its own (violation of rules on incorporation by reference). For objective indicia like praise, the party must tie exhibits to claim features and discuss them in the brief; otherwise the exhibits carry little persuasive weight.
